notes: Replace esr-equality-field-placement with equality-fields-relative-order to test index guidance beyond the ESR acronym. Replace multikey-array-projection-coverage with multikey-expr-index-ineligibility to avoid repeating whole-array fetching. Replace unique-email-duplicate-insert with unique-index-collation-conflict to test a concrete uniqueness case. Replace schema-versions-coexist-in-collection with schema-version-multiple-field-path-indexes and schema-version-dependent-query-paths with schema-version-marker-document-field to avoid overlap with r2 and r5.

cards.statement: MongoDB indexes "profile.city" as an embedded field path when createIndex() uses that key.
cards.explanation: An index key such as {"profile.city":1} indexes the city field inside profile. MongoDB makes that index available for queries on the nested field.

source.title: Create an Index on a Single Field

cards.statement: MongoDB updates the email index when updateOne() changes a document's indexed email value.
cards.explanation: Changing an indexed field updates its corresponding index keys as part of the write. The index continues to reflect the document's current email value.

cards.statement: The {tenant:1,status:1} index supports a query filtered by tenant alone.
cards.explanation: The leading tenant key forms a prefix of {tenant:1,status:1}. MongoDB makes the index available for a tenant filter even when the query omits status.

cards.statement: The {score:-1,name:1} index supports sort({score:1,name:1}) for a query with an empty filter.
cards.explanation: A compound index supplies its specified sort directions or their complete reverse. Sorting both fields ascending changes just the score direction here.
cards.misconception: A compound index independently reverses each field's sort direction.

cards.statement: The {tenant:1,score:1} index supports sorting by score for a query with tenant equality.
cards.explanation: An equality condition fixes the preceding tenant key. MongoDB can then obtain score order from the trailing index key.

source.title: Use Indexes to Sort Query Results

cards.statement: An {email:1} index can cover find({email:"a"},{email:1,phone:1,_id:0}).
cards.explanation: The phone result field is absent from the email index. MongoDB needs document data to return phone, so that index does not cover this query.
cards.misconception: Indexing the filter field suffices to cover a query that returns other fields.

cards.statement: The {email:1} index can cover find({email:null},{email:1,_id:0}).
cards.explanation: A query with equality to null is ineligible for coverage. MongoDB must examine document data even when the filter and returned field occur in the index.
cards.misconception: A null-equality query is covered when its named fields are indexed.

cards.statement: MongoDB's explain() includes index search intervals in an IXSCAN stage of a winning plan.
cards.explanation: The winning plan's IXSCAN node includes the index intervals that MongoDB plans to search. Its position can be nested inside inputStage or queryPlan.
cards.volatilityNote: MongoDB documents explain output fields as subject to change.

cards.statement: MongoDB's explain() totalDocsExamined counts documents that survive the query filter.
cards.explanation: totalDocsExamined includes document examinations that end in rejection by a filter. It measures read work rather than the number of matching results.
cards.misconception: totalDocsExamined reports the result count after filtering.

cards.statement: MongoDB's index guidance puts the most selective equality field first when a query has several equality fields.
cards.explanation: Multiple equality fields may appear in any order relative to each other in a compound index. Their relative placement need not follow a selectivity ranking.
cards.misconception: MongoDB prescribes a selectivity ranking among equality keys in a compound index.

cards.statement: MongoDB's index guidance supports placing a highly selective range field before the sort field.
cards.explanation: A highly selective range can reduce candidate data enough to justify placing it before sort fields. MongoDB documents this ERS alternative to ESR.

cards.statement: MongoDB selects an index as the winning plan as soon as the index is eligible for the query.
cards.explanation: Index eligibility makes an index a possible plan component. MongoDB ranks candidate plans, so another plan may win for the query.
cards.misconception: An eligible index guarantees its own selection by the query optimizer.

cards.statement: MongoDB turns an ordinary index multikey automatically when an indexed field contains an array.
cards.explanation: MongoDB detects array values in indexed fields and records the multikey status. Creating the index uses the ordinary createIndex() method.

source.title: Create an Index on an Array Field

cards.statement: MongoDB can insert {tags:["blue"],codes:["X"]} into a collection with a compound {tags:1,codes:1} index.
cards.explanation: A compound {tags:1,codes:1} index rejects parallel arrays in both fields of one document. That document violates the compound multikey restriction.
cards.misconception: The per-document array restriction permits parallel arrays in a compound index.

cards.statement: MongoDB can accept repeated elements in one document's indexed array under a unique multikey index.
cards.explanation: Repeating a key within the same document is permitted by a unique multikey index. MongoDB stores that repeated index entry once.

cards.statement: Query $elemMatch can let MongoDB intersect lower and upper bounds for an indexed array field.
cards.explanation: For an indexed array, joining range predicates with query $elemMatch lets MongoDB intersect their index bounds into a tighter interval.

cards.statement: MongoDB can verify a candidate's tags value equals ["blue","green"] from multikey entries before fetching it.
cards.explanation: For whole-array equality, multikey entries locate candidates. MongoDB fetches each candidate document to verify its complete array value.
cards.misconception: Multikey entries contain enough information to verify a candidate's full array value.

cards.statement: MongoDB can use a multikey index to resolve a query $expr comparison on the indexed array field.
cards.explanation: A comparison inside query $expr is ineligible for multikey index support. MongoDB evaluates that comparison from document data.
cards.misconception: Query $expr comparisons receive multikey index support for indexed arrays.

cards.statement: In MongoDB 9.0, a running query may fail when a concurrent write makes its referenced indexed field multikey.
cards.explanation: A concurrent multikey transition can raise QueryKilledError in a query referencing that field. MongoDB recommends rerunning the query after the write finishes.
cards.volatilityNote: MongoDB 9.0 introduces this query failure behavior; later releases may revise it.

cards.statement: One text index can serve $text queries across both title and summary fields in a collection.
cards.explanation: A text index may include multiple string fields. Defining title and summary as text keys makes either field available to the same $text search.

cards.statement: The $text query predicate can use a regular ascending string index to supply its word matches.
cards.explanation: The $text query predicate needs a text index. A regular ascending index on the same string field does not satisfy that prerequisite.
cards.misconception: An ordinary string-field index provides the word-search support needed by $text.

cards.statement: The $text search string "coffee cake" combines its unquoted terms with AND matching.
cards.explanation: The unquoted $search value "coffee cake" uses OR between its terms. A document matching either search term qualifies.
cards.misconception: Unquoted words in a $text search string impose AND matching.

cards.statement: The $text query predicate returns matches in descending relevance order by default.
cards.explanation: $text assigns relevance scores but leaves score ordering unspecified. An explicit sort such as {score:{$meta:"textScore"}} requests descending score order.
cards.misconception: A $text predicate implicitly sorts its results by relevance.

cards.statement: The $text query predicate treats words enclosed in double quotes within $search as an exact phrase.
cards.explanation: Double quotes around a multi-word phrase inside the $search value request a phrase match. The words need to appear together in that order.

cards.statement: A unique email index with collation:{locale:"en",strength:2} rejects email:"A@X" when another document has email:"a@x".
cards.explanation: A unique index uses its collation to compare string keys. With English strength 2, changing letter case still produces a duplicate-key conflict.
cards.appliesTo: MongoDB 9.0, ordinary unsharded collection, index collation:{locale:"en",strength:2}

cards.statement: A unique {team:1,email:1} index rejects a repeated email even when the team value differs.
cards.explanation: A compound unique index constrains the complete combination of indexed values. The same email paired with a different team forms a different index key.
cards.misconception: A unique compound index enforces a separate uniqueness constraint on each indexed field.

cards.statement: MongoDB can create a unique {email:1} index despite duplicate email values in separate stored documents.
cards.explanation: Existing duplicate index keys prevent a unique index from being built. Stored documents need to satisfy the constraint before the build can succeed.
cards.misconception: Unique index creation applies its constraint to future writes and accepts existing duplicate keys.

cards.statement: db.c.createIndex({email:1},{unique:true}) gives email:null and missing email the same null index key.
cards.explanation: In this full single-field unique index, an explicit null and an absent email both produce a null key. Those documents compete for the same unique entry.

cards.statement: MongoDB omits active:false documents from an {active:1} index with partialFilterExpression:{active:true}.
cards.explanation: The partial filter determines which documents receive entries in this index. Documents with active:false stay stored in the collection but lack an entry in that index.

cards.statement: The query {email:"a@x"} qualifies for an email index with partialFilterExpression:{active:true}.
cards.explanation: This query can also match inactive documents, so the partial index could omit valid results. Eligible query conditions need to imply the index filter.
cards.misconception: Matching an indexed field makes a query eligible for a partial index even when the query omits the filter condition.

cards.statement: An index on email can use partialFilterExpression:{active:true} even when active is outside the index key.
cards.explanation: A partial index filter can inspect fields outside the key pattern. Here, email determines the key while active determines document inclusion.

cards.statement: A unique email index with partialFilterExpression:{active:true} rejects duplicate emails among inactive documents.
cards.explanation: The unique constraint covers documents matching the partial filter. Documents with active:false fall outside that scope, so their email values can repeat.
cards.misconception: A partial unique index enforces uniqueness for documents outside its filter.

cards.statement: MongoDB treats expiresAt:"2020-01-01T00:00:00Z" as ineligible for TTL expiration on that field.
cards.explanation: TTL expiration examines BSON Date values. A date-looking string remains a string and supplies no eligible date value to the TTL index.

cards.statement: A compound {createdAt:1,userId:1} index can expire documents using expireAfterSeconds.
cards.explanation: MongoDB ignores expireAfterSeconds on a compound index. TTL expiration uses a single-field index.
cards.misconception: A compound index becomes a TTL index when its options include expireAfterSeconds.

cards.statement: MongoDB can calculate TTL expiration from the earliest BSON Date in an indexed array of dates.
cards.explanation: For an indexed array containing dates, the lowest date supplies the TTL expiration threshold. Adding a later date leaves that earlier threshold in effect.

cards.statement: MongoDB removes a TTL-indexed document at the exact instant its indexed date reaches the expiration threshold.
cards.explanation: MongoDB deletes expired documents during background work. An expired document can remain in the collection while that work waits or catches up.
cards.misconception: The TTL expiration threshold is a guaranteed exact deletion deadline.

cards.statement: MongoDB favors embedding bounded child data that an application fetches together with its parent.
cards.explanation: Embedding children with their parent keeps related data fetched together in one record. The application retrieves that group with a single database operation.

source.title: Embedded Data in Your MongoDB Schema

cards.statement: MongoDB favors embedding bounded related values that an application repeatedly changes together.
cards.explanation: Frequently changing related values together is a documented reason to embed them. Keeping that group in one document matches the application's write workload.

source.title: Best Practices for Data Modeling in MongoDB

cards.statement: MongoDB favors embedding a related entity that applications usually query independently of its parent.
cards.explanation: References suit a related entity frequently queried on its own. Keeping its data in a separate document lets the application access the entity independently.
cards.misconception: Embedding is the preferred relationship model even when the related entity has an independent read workload.

source.title: Reference Data in Your MongoDB Schema

cards.statement: MongoDB propagates an entity's source document changes to copies embedded in other documents.
cards.explanation: The application maintains copies in other documents with additional writes. Frequent source changes increase the work needed to keep those copied values consistent.
cards.misconception: MongoDB keeps duplicated values synchronized as an intrinsic consequence of updating their source.

cards.statement: Unbounded embedded arrays pose a performance risk for MongoDB queries as the parent document grows.
cards.explanation: An array that keeps accumulating entries can strain application resources and decrease index performance. The data model needs a plan for that continuing growth.

cards.statement: MongoDB's modeling guidance favors embedding when one parent has a very large number of children.
cards.explanation: MongoDB's modeling guidance points toward references when the child side has high cardinality. Children can live in separate documents linked to their parent.
cards.misconception: A high-cardinality child relationship strengthens the case for embedding the child population in its parent.

source.title: Best Practices for Data Modeling in MongoDB

cards.statement: An application using the Computed pattern stores a derived result for later reads.
cards.explanation: The Computed pattern saves a derived value in MongoDB ahead of reads. The application fetches that stored result instead of computing it again on demand.

cards.statement: Periodic Computed pattern refreshes keep stored summaries current as their source data changes.
cards.explanation: A periodically refreshed computed value can lag source changes made after its last refresh. Reads between refreshes may return an earlier derived result.
cards.misconception: Periodic refresh keeps a stored computed result current with source data at the moment of any read.

cards.statement: For pagination, the Bucket pattern puts a page's related records together in one document.
cards.explanation: Page-sized buckets group records according to the application's pagination needs. A read of the appropriate bucket retrieves the records for one page.

source.title: Group Data with the Bucket Pattern

cards.statement: In the Outlier pattern, MongoDB moves overflow values to another collection when has_extras becomes true.
cards.explanation: The Outlier pattern uses application logic to write overflow values to a separate collection. A has_extras field marks those extras; setting it does not trigger a server-managed move.
cards.misconception: The Outlier pattern's marker activates built-in server handling for overflowing arrays.

source.title: Group Data with the Outlier Pattern

cards.statement: The Schema Versioning Pattern can call for indexes on both field paths when a later document layout moves a field.
cards.explanation: When schema versions store a field at different document paths, supporting queries on those locations may need separate indexes. Index planning follows the stored layouts.

cards.statement: The Schema Versioning Pattern can identify a document's layout through a schemaVersion collection option.
cards.explanation: The application stores schemaVersion as a field in document data. Individual documents carry the marker that identifies their layout.
cards.misconception: The schema-version marker belongs to collection metadata rather than the documents that use different layouts.
